candidateRows: Human behavior is sufficiently deterministic to exclude free will because every action results from an unbroken chain of prior causes.
This states the con side's governing thesis and directly denies the genuinely available alternatives asserted by the motion.
At the outset of his opening, Sapolsky defines determinism as causality extending backward through prior events and applies that account directly to human behavior.
Choices attributed to free will instead reflect interacting causes operating from seconds before an act through development, ancestry, culture, and evolution.
The extended causal sequence supplies the principal empirical support for the con thesis that actions arise from prior conditions rather than free choice.
Sapolsky surveys immediate sensory cues, hunger, hormones, trauma, childhood adversity, fetal conditions, genes, culture, and evolutionary history as influences on behavior.
Biological and environmental explanations form one seamless interacting causal account that leaves no independent space for free will.
The synthesis converts the preceding examples into the direct conclusion that a complete causal continuum excludes free will altogether.
After warning that no single gene, brain region, hormone, or culture explains everything, Sapolsky argues that the disciplines describe interconnected parts of one causal arc.
Free will means that multiple alternatives are genuinely possible and that the person controls which alternative becomes actual.
This defines the pro thesis and contrasts it directly with hard determinism's claim that natural laws and initial conditions permit only one outcome.
Huemer defines free will as alternative possibilities under personal control, defines hard determinism as a single physically determined possibility, and announces his challenge.
Hard determinism conflicts with ordinary judgments and reactive attitudes because reasons, duties, responsibility, pride, guilt, praise, and blame presuppose alternatives.
It supports the pro case by tying alternative possibilities to pervasive normative judgments and responsibility-related attitudes implicated by the motion.

Huemer argues that normative judgments and emotions assume responsibility and available alternatives, while clarifying that determinism would make those attitudes mistaken rather than psychologically impossible.
Without alternative possibilities, rewarding, retributive punishment, deliberation, advice, evaluation, and acting for reasons cease to make sense.
The argument connects free will to deliberation and responsibility practices, directly supporting the motion's claim that freedom matters for responsibility.
Huemer maintains that advice and deliberation require avoidable options, while evaluation and reason-guided action require alternatives among which an agent could act.
Hard determinism is self-defeating because deliberating, arguing, and rationally accepting it invoke norms and alternatives that determinism itself denies.
This is Huemer's principal direct objection: the act of rationally defending determinism allegedly presupposes the agency and normative reasons that the doctrine eliminates.
Huemer invokes earlier formulations of self-defeat, then argues that deciding what to believe, offering reasons, and following rational norms cannot coherently support determinism.
Intuitive appearances are historically and experimentally unreliable, so the felt obviousness of free choice cannot establish that free will exists.
This directly attacks the epistemic foundation Sapolsky attributes to the pro case, using repeated errors and unconscious influences to undermine intuitive certainty.
Huemer's opening appeal to ordinary judgments, deliberative experience, and the apparent necessity of alternative possibilities.
Sapolsky cites discarded intuitive explanations, prejudicial historical beliefs, and priming experiments to argue that people routinely confabulate reasons and misread how behavior arises.
The absence of free will does not prevent change, because organisms and people are changed through fully mechanistic processes rather than choosing change freely.
This answers the practical objection that determinism makes intervention or change incoherent, preserving causal responsiveness without conceding free agency.
Huemer's claim that determinism makes deliberation, advice, reasons, and meaningful efforts to alter conduct incoherent.
Sapolsky distinguishes determinism from fatalistic stasis and argues that conditioning, learning, and rapid psychological updates are causal changes that require no freely choosing self.
Evidence that external conditions influence behavior does not show complete determination, especially when examples involve impairment rather than ordinary reason-responsive decisions.
The reply challenges the main inferential bridge in Sapolsky's empirical case, separating partial causal influence and impaired cases from universal determinism.
Sapolsky's opening inference from numerous biological and environmental influences on behavior to the conclusion that every action is fully determined.
Huemer distinguishes influence from determination and abnormal from normal cases, arguing that hunger or psychiatric impairment does not establish the absence of freedom in well-functioning agents.
Determinism permits change only when that change is itself determined, leaving people unable to control what happens.
The move directly connects causal determination to the absence of control, addressing the central dispute over genuinely available actions.
The earlier claim that determinism is compatible with meaningful change and therefore need not be hopeless.
After defending intuition as a basis for belief, Huemer answers the contention that deterministic systems can still change by distinguishing change from control over change.
Even if abandoning free will makes social life difficult to redesign, rejecting deserved punishment would better reflect how the world works.
The move accepts the practical challenge posed by disbelief in free will while defending its direct implications for blame, punishment, and responsibility.
Huemer's concern that determinism is hopeless and that abandoning responsibility would undermine ordinary social practices.
Sapolsky acknowledges uncertainty about how society would function without praise, blame, reward, and punishment, but treats that difficulty as no reason to retain a false framework.
Purely deterrent and incapacitative punishment cannot explain why framing an innocent ex-convict is wrong while punishing the actual offender is permissible.
The hypothetical is a direct argument that responsibility and desert remain necessary to distinguish justified punishment from expedient harm to an innocent person.
Sapolsky's claim that retribution makes no sense and that abandoning free will should transform punishment practices.
Huemer first notes that determinists can retain deterrence, then argues through a framing case that deterrence and incapacitation alone yield an unacceptable equivalence.
Long-run consequential analysis can reject framing an innocent person without invoking retributive desert because institutional permission to do so causes wider harm.
The response supplies a non-retributive explanation of the case's wrongness, challenging Huemer's claim that only deserved punishment can distinguish the offenders.
Huemer's framing hypothetical offered to show that deterrence and incapacitation cannot replace retributive justification.
Sapolsky broadens the time horizon of the hypothetical, comparing it with organ harvesting and arguing that systemic consequences defeat the apparent narrow utility.
A secret one-off framing remains unjust even without adverse systemic consequences, so the moral distinction depends on desert and retributive reasoning.
The move isolates the proposed moral intuition from institutional side effects and makes retributive desert the claimed explanation of the remaining difference.
Sapolsky's argument that long-term social consequences explain why framing an innocent person is impermissible.
Huemer stipulates a single undiscovered framing to remove loss of confidence and other systemic effects, then appeals to the injustice suffered by the innocent person.
Scientific explanations have repeatedly removed blame and retribution from misunderstood behavior, producing a more humane world rather than social collapse.
The historical induction supports the con side's responsibility thesis by arguing that causal understanding systematically displaces blame with humane treatment.
Huemer's contention that retribution is necessary to make justified moral and punitive distinctions.
Sapolsky contrasts older punitive interpretations of disease and behavior with later causal explanations, arguing that diminished responsibility has repeatedly improved treatment.
Past errors about responsibility do not justify general skepticism about present beliefs unless those errors share a substantive premise with the current belief.
The move attacks the inferential basis of Sapolsky's historical case, arguing that mere similarity in apparent obviousness cannot undermine present responsibility judgments.
Sapolsky's historical projection that future people will regard current responsibility practices as seriously mistaken and inhumane.
Huemer argues that universal fallibility cannot rationally require abandoning current best judgments and demands a tighter evidential connection between past and present errors.
Because no neuron's contribution to behavior can be shown independent of biological and environmental causes, expanding causal knowledge warrants deep caution about blame.
This is a direct mechanistic challenge to libertarian agency coupled to the debate's responsibility question and the moral cost of treating causally shaped conduct as freely chosen.
Huemer's claim that known influences do not establish determination and that historical errors cannot broadly defeat current responsibility beliefs.
Sapolsky asks for behavior independent of hormones, genes, development, and environment, then invokes the rapid growth of such findings and the harms caused by misplaced certainty.
Absent decisive scientific proof either way, the rational default is to accept the appearance of possessing free will until compelling contrary evidence emerges.
The move supplies the pro side's epistemic burden of proof, grounding belief in free agency despite incomplete prediction and extensive evidence of causal influence.
Sapolsky's mechanistic challenge and claim that accumulating causal knowledge makes confidence in free agency and blame unwarranted.
Huemer allows that perfect prediction could support determinism but notes that neither side has such proof, so he applies a general presumption in favor of appearances.
Mechanistic testing repeatedly exposes false intuitions, and existing evidence already shows substantially less freedom in morally important domains than people assume.
The move directly rebuts intuition-based confidence in free will and argues that current causal evidence is already sufficient to revise responsibility judgments.
Huemer's defense of appearances and moral intuitions as the necessary basis for belief in free will and moral progress.
Sapolsky argues that interventions can distinguish accurate from inaccurate intuitions, invokes counterintuitive scientific discoveries, and urges revision of current responsibility practices.
A free choice can be explained by the agent's reasons even though, at some point, why that reason prevailed has no further determining explanation.
It directly addresses whether libertarian choices are inexplicable brute facts and distinguishes reasons-based explanation from deterministic necessitation.
The questioner's suggestion that a genuinely free choice may be an unexplained brute fact.
After both speakers distinguish scientific explanation from predictability, Huemer returns to the question of how a free choice can have reasons without being fully determined.
Behavior always has prior causes, while quantum indeterminacy cannot ground free will because microscopic indeterminate states cannot scale up to influence persons or societies.
It states the deterministic alternative to Huemer's unexplained decision point and blocks quantum indeterminacy as a proposed source of agency.
Huemer's claim that explanation eventually ends with what the agent simply decides to do.
Immediately after Huemer locates an explanatory stopping point in free decision, Sapolsky insists that prior causes continue and addresses a familiar indeterminist escape route.
Gratitude can be explained through the adaptive value of reciprocity and through proximal neural differences, without presupposing that beneficiaries freely chose to help.
The move supports the deterministic account of responsibility-related emotions by explaining their existence without relying on freely chosen altruism.
The questioner's challenge that gratitude lacks a rationale if helpers had no choice about helping.
An audience question asks why gratitude would evolve if assistance is not freely chosen; Sapolsky supplies both distal evolutionary and proximal biological explanations.
No philosophical conception of free will survives what biology and environmental causation reveal, so practices of blame, reward, and punishment require major reconsideration.
It gives Sapolsky's direct reason for rejecting compatibilism and connects causal determination to the debate's central issue of moral responsibility.
The compatibilist position implied by the question asking why hard determinism is necessary.
Asked why he is not merely a compatibilist, Sapolsky argues that contemporary causal knowledge excludes every meaningful form of free will and changes responsibility practices.
If determinism were established, preserving the ordinary concept of free will through compatibilism would be preferable to denying that every paradigm free action is free.
It explains Huemer's methodological resistance to hard determinism by tying an adequate analysis of freedom to ordinary paradigm instances of voluntary action.
Sapolsky's hard-incompatibilist conclusion that causal determination leaves no meaningful free will.
Following Sapolsky's rejection of all compatibilist accounts, Huemer explains how conceptual analysis should respect paradigm applications and states his fallback position.
If doing otherwise would require a different past, then one cannot do otherwise; because determinism imposes that condition universally, it conflicts with free will.
This is a direct consequence argument from determinism to the absence of alternative possibilities and hence to incompatibility with ordinary free will.
The compatibilist possibility that actions can remain free even when antecedent causes determine them.
Huemer moves from conceptual methodology to a concrete grade example, extracting a general principle about past conditions and applying it to determinism.
Failures to believe propositions contradicted by conclusive evidence do not establish general doxastic involuntarism or show an absence of control over belief.
It defends the premise that belief can involve control, which is necessary for Huemer's argument from rational deliberation against determinist self-understanding.
The doxastic-involuntarist objection that people cannot choose any of their beliefs.
An audience question challenges Huemer's appeal to choosing beliefs; he narrows the familiar counterexamples to cases where evidence is effectively conclusive.
Reasoning about what to believe is a deliberative choice process analogous to weighing reasons for and against ordinary actions.
The analogy supplies positive support for control over belief rather than merely rebutting examples, reinforcing his challenge to deterministic accounts of rational assent.
The objection that belief formation is involuntary even if people possess free will in other domains.
After limiting involuntarist counterexamples, Huemer argues affirmatively that weighing epistemic reasons resembles the acknowledged choice structure of practical deliberation.
The practical meaning of 'should' presupposes capability and cannot be reduced to the claim that an outcome would simply be better.
The semantic argument protects the inference from normative claims to alternative possibilities, linking ordinary advice and responsibility to genuine ability.
The proposed deterministic reinterpretation of 'should' as merely meaning that an outcome would be better.
The question proposes definitions of normative language compatible with no alternatives; Huemer uses impossible tasks to argue that such definitions distort ordinary practical usage.
A microphysical determinism in which electrical and chemical brain events determine belief cannot explain responsiveness to truth or epistemic reasons.
It addresses whether deterministic belief formation can remain rationally evidence-responsive, a key challenge to using argument as support for determinism.
The objection that deterministic causes could make beliefs follow good epistemic reasons and evidence.
In the debate's final substantive exchange, Huemer distinguishes determinism generally from a microphysical version whose causal elements lack sensitivity to normative epistemic properties.
